hints: Focus on which functional group actually reacts with HCN in the presence of cyanide catalyst.
Remember that HCN addition adds exactly one extra carbon to the molecule as the -CN group, so work backwards from 4 carbons in R to find carbons in Q.
Check each structure to find a 3-carbon aldehyde or ketone, since carboxylic acids and halogenoalkanes do not form cyanohydrins.
walkthrough:
**Recall the HCN reaction**

Think like this, HCN adds across the C=O bond of aldehydes and ketones to make a hydroxynitrile called a cyanohydrin.

General equation:
$$\text{R}_2\text{C=O} + \text{HCN} \rightarrow \text{R}_2\text{C(OH)(CN)}$$

**Use the carbon count**

The CN group brings one new carbon into the product, so product R has one more carbon than starting Q.

Calculation rule:
$$\text{carbons in Q} = \text{carbons in R} - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3$$
So Q must be a 3-carbon aldehyde or ketone.

**Count carbons and identify Q**

Option D is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, propanal. It has 3 carbons and an aldehyde C=O, so it will add HCN to give a 4-carbon cyanohydrin $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CN}$. That matches perfectly.

options.A: Incorrect. This is propanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. Carboxylic acids do not undergo nucleophilic addition with HCN to form cyanohydrins, so no reaction to give R occurs.
options.B: Incorrect. This is butan-2-one, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. It would react with HCN, but it already has 4 carbons, so its cyanohydrin would have 5 carbons, not 4.
options.C: Incorrect. This is 1-chlorobutane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$. Halogenoalkanes do not react with HCN by addition, they undergo nucleophilic substitution under different conditions, and this would not fit the carbon count.
options.D: Correct. This is propanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, a 3-carbon aldehyde. Aldehydes react readily with HCN to form a cyanohydrin, adding one carbon to give a 4-carbon product $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CN}$.
